items.title: US high court rulings have been 'destructive to democracy,' Justice Kagan says
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 20 (Reuters) - US Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan on Tuesday said the court's conservative majority has undermined democracy and "created a ​race to the bottom" in how congressional districts are drawn.

Kagan, one of the court's three liberals, told students at ‌Catholic University's law school that the conservatives have enabled increased political polarization by not reining in partisan gerrymandering, which involves states redrawing the boundaries of electoral districts based on the partisan leanings of voters to boost a political party's candidates.

In recent years, Kagan said, "both political parties have been engaged in a race ​to the bottom in terms of doing these partisan gerrymanders, effectively depriving masses of citizens of their rights to voting ​equality."

Partisan gerrymandering is driving political candidates "toward the extremes, because the only thing anybody has to worry about ⁠anymore is being primaried," Kagan said.

"It is making what I think is unfortunately a too polarized country even more so," Kagan said. "In ​this election, and the next election, we are seeing large states with substantial numbers of people who vote for Republicans and who ​vote for Democrats, and the states are going to be tried to turn all red or all blue in a way that I think is very destructive to our democracy."

The court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority, in April gutted a pillar of the Voting Rights Act, a landmark 1965 civil rights law ​that aimed to prevent racial discrimination in voting.

That ruling prompted a frenzied round of redistricting across the South to eliminate US House of Representatives ​districts where Black voters make up a majority or near-majority, as Republican-led states scrambled to take advantage of the decision. President Donald Trump's Republican Party ‌is seeking ⁠to retain control of Congress in the November midterm elections.

At Trump's urging, Republican-governed Texas redrew its electoral map last year in an effort to flip Democratic-held US House seats, while Democratic-led California then reconfigured its map to target Republican-held House seats.

Kagan, an appointee of former Democratic President Barack Obama, said the court's conservatives did not appreciate the real-world impact of their April voting rights decision, or their June decision that struck down a cap on ​the amount of money parties can ​spend on campaigns with input ⁠from candidates.

"I think part of the reason why the court got it wrong was a lack of the appropriate concern or understanding of the consequences of their decisions," Kagan said.

“I do think in all ​these areas the court has blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on ​how the political ⁠system works and has created a democracy that doesn’t work as well as it should,” she added.

Kagan added that the June decision on campaign finance regulation has created opportunities for donors to corrupt candidates.

"The one place where the court has allowed campaign finance regulation to operate is to ⁠prevent quid ​pro quo corruption, kind of money for favors, and the court never seems ​to see the opportunities for doing exactly that," Kagan said.

“I think you know the people of America look around this political system and think that all this money, ​chasing all these political candidates, is a nightmare, and they’re right,” she said.

items.title: Explainer: Three issues defining the 2026 US midterm elections
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, October 20 - President Donald Trump’s record-low popularity, voter frustration over the cost of living and a fierce immigration fight are shaping the November 3 midterm elections, which will determine whether Republicans keep control of Congress or Democrats gain the power to challenge his administration.

Republicans hold narrow majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to ​take control of each chamber.

The outcome will hinge on a relatively small number of competitive races, but the campaigns are being shaped nationally by Trump himself and voter ‌concerns over affordability and immigration.

Here is a look at the three issues defining the election:

The president has put himself front and center in the closing stretch of the campaign cycle despite his record-low popularity, with upcoming rallies in Florida, Iowa, Michigan and Texas. Trump's approval rating has fallen to an all-time low 31%, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll. Yet he has repeatedly urged voters to pretend he's on the ballot, an effort that could motivate Democrats and independents to ​rally against his party despite the message being aimed at increasing turnout among Trump's base.

Democrats have said Trump has broken his campaign promises to lower costs and end wars. They have ​vowed to tackle an affordability agenda to reduce Americans' cost of living and hold the administration accountable for alleged corruption if voters give them control ⁠of either chamber.

Voters have consistently ranked the cost of living as the top issue this election cycle. Half of registered voters surveyed in a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll cited the cost of living as the most ​important factor in how they will vote. In the same poll, voters highlighted healthcare, gasoline, food and housing as the top household bills lawmakers should focus on.

Republicans' top legislative achievement was a tax cut ​extension that slashed roughly $1 trillion in spending for Medicaid, the government health insurance program for low-income Americans, and other health programs. Democrats last year forced a government shutdown over a failed effort to extend expiring health subsidies that benefited 24 million Americans.

Gas prices have spiked since the US and Israel launched military strikes on Iran in February. The national average price of gas is $4.28 — $1.20 higher than it was a year ago, according to AAA. The average cost of ​diesel is $6.32 — a $2.70 increase from a year earlier.

Grocery costs are up 1.8% over the past year, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics data on consumer prices. Federal Housing Finance Agency data show ​home prices rose 2.1% over the past year. Congress passed a bipartisan housing bill earlier this year. It became law without Trump's signature.

Preliminary data from the Department of Homeland Security showed a 95% drop in migrants apprehended ‌at the southwest ⁠border compared to former President Joe Biden's administration. The agency said there have been no Border Patrol releases the entire fiscal year for the first time ever.

But fatal encounters with federal immigration agents have occurred in Maine, Minnesota and Texas. The backlash to the death of two US citizens in Minnesota pulled many Democrats in competitive primaries to the left this year, with some candidates calling for the impeachment of then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and others saying Immigration and Customs Enforcement should be abolished.

Democrats and Republicans sparred over immigration funding this year in a stalemate that forced Republicans to unilaterally pass a $70 billion ​bill to fund ICE and the Border Patrol ​for the remainder of Trump's presidency. Republicans ⁠counter Democrats' criticism by saying Democrats support open borders.

Federal immigration officials also raided the Washington home of Democratic US Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota this month, drawing widespread condemnation from Democrats. A person familiar with the case against Omar told Reuters one potential aim of the investigation could be to strip her of US ​citizenship and deport her.

Artificial intelligence and data centers, cryptocurrency, abortion and Israel could also influence voters in individual races. In Ohio's Senate race, ​for example, Democratic nominee Sherrod ⁠Brown has labeled Republican Senator Jon Husted the face of data centers, and the crypto super PAC Defend American Jobs has spent more than $46 million to reelect Husted over Brown, a former US senator who chaired the chamber's Banking Committee.

In Maine's Senate race, Democratic nominee Troy Jackson is hoping voters don't forget that Republican Senator Susan Collins helped confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court, which later overturned the federal right to ⁠abortion. Collins is ​on the election ballot for the first time since the high court made abortion a state issue rather than a ​federal right.

In Michigan, Republican nominee Mike Rogers has indicated he would accept help from a pro-Israel super PAC that spent more than $30 million backing Democratic US Representative Haley Stevens in her unsuccessful primary against Abdul El-Sayed, who now faces Rogers in the ​general election. The group has already spent more than $280,000 on mailers against El-Sayed.

Earlier this week, Trump endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection.

items.title: Trump, Bloomberg ramp up spending ahead of midterms
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 20 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he would ​spend more than $400 million on Republican campaign efforts, while ‌the New York Times reported that former New York City mayor Michael Bloomberg was spending $80 million to help Democrats ahead of the November ​3 midterm congressional elections.

The financial commitments come as Democrats seek ​to win control of Congress from Trump's Republicans in the ⁠November 3 midterm elections.

"I have spent, or will be ​spending, over 400 Million Dollars by Election Day. More than 300 ​Million Dollars has already been spent on Advertising, Direct and Indirect Voter Contact, Rallies, Rally Arenas, Telerallies, Get Out the Vote Programs, Election Integrity, ​and more," Trump said in a social media post.

Trump's super ​PAC, MAGA Inc., and an affiliated group, No Going Back PAC, have ‌spent ⁠at least $226 million on the elections so far, campaign filings show.

Bloomberg's team told the New York Times that he was sending about $80 million to Democrats in September and October.

Bloomberg's office did ​not immediately respond ​to a ⁠request for comment.

The New York Times said at least $50 million of Bloomberg’s money was being used ​for House races, including $24 million for Everytown for ​Gun ⁠Safety, a group Bloomberg co-founded. He was also giving $16 million to House Majority PAC, the main super PAC aligned with House Democratic ⁠leadership.

Reuters has ​not independently verified the spending by ​Bloomberg.

items.title: US Social Security Agency corrects nearly 15% of records in database cleanup
items.content_html: Oct 20 (Reuters) - The US Social Security Administration said on Tuesday that it had corrected records for nearly 15% ​of all active Social Security numbers, adding ‌missing death and citizenship information, as part of the Trump administration's effort to prevent fraud in the benefits program.

items.title: Trump drops threats against Canadian jet maker Bombardier, citing US jobs
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON/MONTREAL, Oct 20 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump has dropped threats against Canadian jet maker Bombardier (BBDb.TO), opens new tab to ban it ​from the US market and instead vowed to take "good care" of the company's workers in Kansas.

‌Trump's threats in September against Bombardier became a political issue in Kansas, where it employs 1,500 workers in Wichita. The threatened ban prompted calls to the White House from Kansas lawmakers including Republican Senator Roger Marshall, who ​is facing a tough re-election bid.

"We're going to take care of Bombardier," Trump told ​12 News in Kansas, citing Marshall's involvement.

At a speech Monday, Trump said he ⁠would help Bombardier.

"I'm going to be helping a certain air company get themselves straightened away... ​I'll be helping them because I always viewed them as a Canadian company," Trump said. "But now I ​find out they have a presence here, and we're not hurting them if they're in Kansas. So we'll take care of those people and the jobs."

Bombardier's shares rose 4% Tuesday after Trump's comments. The White House declined ​to comment and referred questions to Trump's TV interview.

Bombardier, which in 1990 acquired Learjet and established ​its US headquarters in Kansas, has 3,500 jobs in the US, more than 40% of which are in ‌Wichita.

Bombardier recently ⁠announced a North American Learning Center in Kansas and has said it workforce in the state is growing. Last week, it announced a $50 million investment in Wichita, where it has its defense headquarters, and also plans to open a facility in Fort Wayne, Indiana.

Last month, the Trump administration ​banned a broad swath of ​Canadian alcoholic beverages, ⁠motorcycles and dairy products from import, effective September 29, but took no action against Bombardier.

The action came after Canada's own retaliatory tariffs on US goods ​took effect in early September. Those were prompted after Washington imposed tariffs ​on some $20 ⁠billion of Canadian goods in August, after several rounds of negotiations collapsed.

Reuters reported last month it was not immediately clear how Trump could bar Bombardier private jets from being delivered to American customers since ⁠they ​have been approved by the US Federal Aviation Administration.

Threats by ​Trump in February to decertify Bombardier aircraft over a certification spat involving US rival Gulfstream Aerospace (GD.N), opens new tab never materialized, with regulator ​Transport Canada eventually approving the American-made jets.

items.title: US judge dismisses Sam Altman's sister's sexual abuse lawsuit
items.content_html:
Oct 20 (Reuters) - Sam Altman on Tuesday won the dismissal ​of a civil lawsuit filed by his sister accusing the ‌OpenAI co-founder and chief executive of repeated sexual abuse more than two decades ago, an accusation he denies.

In dismissing Annie Altman's lawsuit, US District Judge ​Zachary Bluestone wrote that she had refused to appear for ​an independent medical examination despite warnings that failure to do ⁠so would result in the case's dismissal.

Laura Politi, a lawyer for ​Annie Altman, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. ​Santos Perez, a lawyer who previously represented Annie Altman in the case but withdrew this month, said in a statement, "I am no longer authorized to comment on ​this case but I continue to believe in Annie."

Lawyers for Sam ​Altman did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Sam Altman became a ‌face ⁠of the artificial intelligence boom after the chatbot ChatGPT was released in 2022.

Annie Altman brought her lawsuit in St. Louis, Missouri, federal court in January 2025.

She accused her brother of sexually abusing and raping her ​between 1997 and ​2006 at ⁠the family home in suburban Clayton, Missouri, starting when she was 3 and he was 12. She ​said the last acts of sexual abuse and rape ​occurred when ⁠Sam Altman was an adult. He is now 41.

The Altman family has said Annie Altman has mental health challenges and received financial support. Sam ⁠Altman has ​said she began accusing him on social ​media of sexual abuse after the family rejected her demands for more funds.

items.title: Ahead of elections, Bessent says a Democrat-led Congress could do little to stop Trump agenda
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 20 (Reuters) - US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday that there was not much a Democrat-led House of Representatives could do ​to stop the Trump administration's agenda.

"I think there's very little," ‌Bessent said in an interview on 2Way TV two weeks ahead of November's midtermelections.

"We have very durable tariff authorities," he said, referring to Democrats' opposition to Trump ​broadly imposing tariffs on goods imported from countries around the world.

Control ​of Congress is at stake as voters head to ⁠the polls on November 3 to choose members of the House ​of Representatives and Senate and governors in states across the country. The ​Republican Party currently has a narrow majority in both the Senate and the House of Representatives.

The election comes as Trump's approval rating has dipped over his handling of ​the high cost of living for Americans during the US-Israeli war ​with Iran that has raised fuel prices.

Bessent said the Treasury's effort to isolate Iraneconomically ‌was ⁠working.

"We haven't seen any loadings at the Iranian oil facility on Kharg Island since August. Iran currently has no oil on the water," he said.

"Panic is starting to set in ... I don't know whether it's ​going to take ​four more weeks ⁠or eight more weeks, but at a point, their economy will go nonlinear," he said.

Bessent also said ​he had not heard whether Russian President Vladimir Putin ​had accepted ⁠Trump's invitation to attend the G20 summit in Florida in December.

"I haven't seen his RSVP yea or nay yet," Bessent said.

Trump has said ⁠Russia ​has agreed to supply diesel to global ​markets, and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel designed to deprive Moscow ​of revenue for its war in Ukraine.

items.title: US single-family housing starts plunge; building permits hit 3-1/2-year low
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 20 (Reuters) - US single-family homebuilding fell sharply in September and permits for future construction tumbled to a 3-1/2-year low as higher mortgage rates suppressed demand, suggesting residential investment resumed its declining trend ​in the third quarter.

The report from the Commerce Department on Tuesday followed on the heels of a National Association of Home Builders survey on Monday showing sentiment among single-family homebuilders plunged ‌in October to the lowest level since June 2012.

The deterioration in sentiment was blamed on rising material costs and mortgage rates as well as more expensive diesel and "worsening" labor conditions amid an immigration crackdown. Expensive mortgages have combined with still-elevated home prices to create what economists have called an affordability crisis, which is dominating campaign messaging ahead of the crucial November 3 midterm elections.

President Donald Trump earlier this year refused to sign a bipartisan housing affordability bill, calling it "a big yawn" as he ​pressed Congress, including fellow Republicans resisting his demands, to first pass separate and contentious voting requirements legislation. The housing bill became law without Trump's signature.

"The weakness in housing starts is not surprising. Even ​if homebuilders were putting up new houses, who could afford to buy them?" said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. "The housing market is about to go ⁠into a deep sleep unless Washington can do a 180 on its policies and make the cost of a new home more affordable."

Single-family housing starts, which account for the bulk of homebuilding, dropped 4.6% to a ​seasonally adjusted annual rate of 859,000 units last month, the lowest level since September 2025, the Commerce Department's Census Bureau said.

Homebuilding fell over the month in the South, Midwest and West regions, but increased in the ​Northeast. Single-family starts rose 2.6% on a year-on-year basis in September.

Mortgage rates have surged in recent weeks, with the 30-year fixed rate averaging 7.40% last week, the highest level in nearly three years, data from mortgage finance firm Freddie Mac showed. The higher borrowing costs are tracking Treasury yields as the US-Israeli war with Iran fans inflation.

Slumping sales have led to a glut of new unsold houses on the market, further reducing the incentive for developers to break ground on new single-family housing projects. ​Despite the overhang of new single-family homes, there is a national housing shortage, which is keeping home prices elevated.

Single-family building permits decreased 4.0% to a rate of 845,000 units, the lowest level since ​March 2023. Permits fell in the Northeast, Midwest and South regions, but were unchanged in the West. They dropped 4.8% year-on-year in September.

Residential investment rebounded in the second quarter, also reflecting renovations, making a small contribution to gross domestic product. ‌The rise ⁠followed five straight quarterly declines. Housing's share of gross domestic product is small, allowing the economy to continue expanding.

Morgan Stanley estimated that residential investment contracted at a 4.0% annualized rate in the third quarter. Economic growth estimates for the quarter stayed just above a 3.0% pace. The economy grew at a 2.2% rate in the April-June quarter. The government is due to publish its advance estimate of third-quarter GDP next week.

Some economists said the building of data centers to support AI technology was worsening construction worker shortages. A separate report from the National Association of Realtors showed pending home sales crumbled to a record low in September.

But some economists viewed the ​slump in single-family homebuilding as necessary given the inventory ​bloat, with the NAHB survey also showing buyer ⁠traffic slumping in October to the lowest level since April 2012.

"So, if builders just proceeded without making an adjustment, inventories would quickly back up," said Stephen Stanley, chief US economist at Santander US Capital Markets. "Hopefully, the slower pace of starts will prevent the market from getting too far out of balance."

The number of ​single-family houses approved for construction that are yet to be started was unchanged at a near 4-1/2-year high of 151,000 units, while completions fell 2.4% to ​a rate of 840,000 units -- ⁠the lowest level since May 2020. The inventory of single-family housing under construction was flat at 587,000 units.

Starts for housing projects with five units or more, a very volatile segment, plummeted 7.2% to a rate of 349,000 units in September. Multifamily housing starts plunged 25.9% on a year-over-year basis. Overall housing starts decreased 5.2% to a pace of 1.221 million units. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast starts dropping to a rate of 1.305 million units.

They declined ⁠7.4% on a ​year-over-year basis in September. Building permits for multifamily housing projects increased 5.9% to a rate of 503,000 units last month. Overall ​building permits slipped 0.2% to a rate of 1.400 million units. Economists had forecast permits falling to a rate of 1.395 million units.

Permits dropped 3.0% on a year-over-year basis in September.

"Our best assessment is that starts will falter in the months ahead until the ​energy shock is better understood," said Carl Weinberg, chief economist at High Frequency Economics. "So don't bet on residential construction to recover anytime soon."

items.title: Iran prolongs talks in stalemate to influence US midterms, officials say
items.content_html:
DUBAI, Oct 20 (Reuters) - Iran has deliberately prolonged talks with the US to try to weaken Donald Trump politically ahead of November's US midterm elections, senior officials say, while fears of renewed military action and deep distrust of Washington have reinforced Tehran's reluctance to strike a quick deal to end ​the war.

Three senior Iranian officials and an Iranian insider, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Tehran was convinced the US president was ready to resort to renewed attacks to try to ‌break the stalemate in the eight-month-old war.

"Iran is preparing for renewed Israeli and US attacks, not for a deal with America to end the war," one of the officials said. "The clerical establishment is determined not to give Trump a political victory."

Tehran analyst Saeed Leylaz said that, by prolonging the talks, "Iran is influencing the US election without taking any unlawful action".

The war, which began in February when the US and its ally Israel launched strikes on Iran, has helped drive ​Trump’s approval rating to a record low as polls suggest that Americans worried about high gasoline prices will punish his Republican Party in the November 3 congressional elections.

Trump has repeatedly said he expects oil ​prices to drop after the elections, but has not offered a detailed plan to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global ⁠energy shipping route effectively closed by Iran since the war began.

Iranian attacks both threatened and real have kept ship traffic through the strait to a trickle, while a US maritime blockade and trade sanctions have cut ​off Iran's oil export revenues and exacerbated growing domestic economic woes.

With Tehran refusing to make concessions it believes could benefit Trump politically, there is little chance of a breakthrough before the elections, the officials said.

Under pressure from ​Israel, Washington wants Iran’s decades-long nuclear programme - which Iran says is purely peaceful and Western powers allege has military dimensions - on the table from the outset.

For its part, Tehran insists that its conditions under a "seven-day plan" must be met before nuclear negotiations begin. And it offers no prospect of giving up the leverage over the Strait of Hormuz that the conflict prompted it to seize.

Iran's Foreign Ministry and the US White House did not respond to Reuters requests for comment.

Iran’s proposal, conveyed through Qatari mediators, offered to reopen the strait within seven days, albeit under Iranian control, provided that Washington lifted its maritime blockade, eased restrictions on Iranian oil exports, released frozen assets and ended ​hostilities on all fronts.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that the offer remained on the table, with messages being exchanged through mediators.

Tehran's view that Washington cannot be trusted to commit to diplomacy stems from the attacks on ‌Iran that ⁠have derailed previous negotiations, one Iranian official said.

In June 2025, an Israeli attack wrecked plans for a sixth round of US-Iran nuclear talks in Oman. And last February, the US and Israel launched their war just after another round of talks ended, with further technical discussions scheduled.

Maintaining a state somewhere between war and peace through the US midterms allows Iran to sustain pressure on Washington while reiterating its commitment to diplomacy.

Trump has said the US will not bomb Iran again before November 3. However, the officials said Tehran continues to expect that bombing will resume, sooner or later.

Alex Vatanka, director of the Iran program at the Middle East Institute ​in Washington, said the clerical establishment clearly wanted to ​hurt Trump politically.

"But the fundamental issue is ⁠that Tehran believes that Trump is interested in regime change ... and following Israeli Prime Minister (Benjamin) Netanyahu’s policy of seeking to bring down Iran’s ruling establishment," he said.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth discussed Iran with Netanyahu on Monday, three Israeli officials said, in an unannounced visit to Israel a week before a parliamentary election in ​which Netanyahu's position is at risk.

Iran’s strategy of keeping negotiations alive without rushing towards agreement comes at ​a cost.

Prolonged uncertainty is weighing ⁠on Iran’s already crippled economy and wearing down public patience. Thousands were killed at the turn of the year when the security forces crushed spiralling anti-government protests.

Annual inflation hit 73.6% in September, according to the Statistical Centre of Iran, and the rial currency has fallen nearly 35% against the dollar since Washington reapplied its naval blockade in July.

Iran’s seaborne crude exports fell to zero in the second week of September from a 14-day average of 230,000 ⁠barrels per day ​at the start of the month, and remained there as of October 5, according to energy intelligence platform Vortexa.

But the leadership's ​distrust of Washington extends beyond the current conflict to existential concerns. Iran believes the US has repeatedly broken agreements even when Tehran honoured its commitments, Leylaz said, leaving little confidence that any comprehensive deal would endure.

“Reaching a sustainable deal with the US, even after ​the Trump administration, is no longer possible because of the deepened distrust,” Leylaz said. "Nothing will go back to the pre-war status quo."

items.title: Could disillusioned Kansas voters send their first Democrat to the US Senate in 94 years?
items.content_html:
GARDEN CITY, Kansas, Oct 20 (Reuters) - The last time the state of Kansas sent a Democrat to the US Senate, the Great Depression was ravaging the state, wheat prices had collapsed and drought was turning the Great Plains into the Dust Bowl.

Some 94 years later, Kansas may do it again.

Democratic ​candidate Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor, is running neck and neck with Republican US Senator Roger Marshall, based on both a New York Times/Siena Poll, opens new tab and Emerson College Polling, opens new tab, in a state that Republican President Donald Trump won ‌in 2024 with more than 57% of the vote.

The unexpectedly competitive race reflects strains in the Republican heartland, where Democrats are betting that soaring farm costs, including near-record-high diesel, and discontent with Trump's immigration crackdown can revive the region's progressive populist tradition.

In the converted grain bin that serves as an office for Vance and Louise Ehmke's wheat farm and seed business, John Brown, the abolitionist who took up arms against slavery in Kansas, stares down from a reproduction of a famous painting.

In 1885, 20 years after the Civil War, Vance Ehmke’s ancestors started farming in western Kansas. But now, climbing costs ​linked to the US-Israeli war on Iran have him contemplating a dark future for his farm and others around it.

“During the past year, we have seen fuel prices just darn near double,” Ehmke said. “That’s cost us $50,000 of unexpected expenses.”

Fuel and fertilizer prices have shot up dramatically since the war started in February, with diesel used to power farm equipment up 70% since the war began.

Those rising costs have reverberated in ⁠states like Kansas, Iowa and Nebraska, where agriculture dominates local economies.

In Iowa, opinion polls show Republican US Representative Ashley Hinson in a tight Senate race with Democrat Josh Turek for the seat being vacated by Republican Joni Ernst.

Hinson called last month for an "immediate end" ​to the Iran war in a social media post that said Iowans "shouldn't have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war."

In Nebraska, Republican Senator Pete Ricketts faces a competitive race against independent Dan Osborn, despite Trump winning the ​state by more than 20 points in 2024.

Democrats need to pick up four US Senate seats to win control of the chamber.

Trump, Vice President JD Vance and other leading Republicans have stumped for at-risk candidates in the Midwest region.

Trump pledged in Nebraska this month to expand access to tax-exempt diesel fuel and, in a Wichita-area rally on Monday, said the US Department of Agriculture would launch a "harvest fuel relief program" to provide farmers with $8 billion to offset diesel costs during the harvest season.

Hamilton still has an uphill climb with many rural Kansas voters. Not ​far from the Ehmkes is another farm owned by Ron Suppes, a Republican who supports Marshall.

“We’ve had high diesel prices in prior years. I don’t know if it matters which administration,” he said.

“I’ll put up with the pain for a while."

Another Trump priority ​hit the Kansas meatpacking industry in late September, when Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrested 104 people in Dodge City, Garden City, Liberal and surrounding areas, according to the US Attorney's Office for the District of Kansas.

Amid voter anger over high beef prices, the raids slowed operations at ‌major processors including ⁠Cargill and National Beef as some employees stayed home for fear of arrest. The raids may also have affected the traditionally conservative politics of those towns.

Wichita State University's IKE Lab found a significant jump in September voter registrations in counties where the ICE raids took place, researcher and professor Alexandra Middlewood said.

Oscar Soto, a grocery store owner in Dodge City, was shocked when he began seeing social media reports of ICE agents flooding his town on September 22. He joined with a group of community organizers to take meals to families afraid to leave home or whose providers had been arrested.

He said what he saw that week as he volunteered inspired him to register to vote for the first time at the age of 39.

“What can I do to help make ​any difference at all?" he said he asked himself. "And the one ​thing I landed on was voting."

He said he planned ⁠to vote for the Democrat.

In the 2024 election, Trump won nearly half the Hispanic vote, but an October 5 Reuters/Ipsos poll showed just 24% of Hispanic Americans now approve of Trump's performance in the White House. Hispanic voters made up more than 9% of Kansas voters in 2024, according to the Pew Research Center.

Marshall's campaign has criticized Hamilton over an incident in which a ​volunteer at a camp connected to his church was accused of molesting two teenage boys. Church leaders initially only investigated the incident internally, later reporting it to police when the ​volunteer returned to the camp and was ⁠again accused of inappropriate behavior.

Hamilton has since said the church should have gone to police first and that it changed its policy after the incident to require that.

Hamilton’s campaign, in turn, has highlighted a September New York Times report that Marshall, an obstetrician before entering politics, sued more than 700 patients over unpaid medical bills. Marshall said he had followed typical collection practices.

Marshall’s campaign did not respond to a request for an interview but issued a statement that said in part he had delivered for farmers, cut middle-class taxes and secured the ⁠border, and sought to ​tie Hamilton to national Democrats, calling him a “Chuck Schumer-funded Democrat,” referring to the Senate minority leader from New York.

In Garden City on October 9, a ​group of voters awaited Hamilton’s visit in a small café, including Michael Shull, a retired pediatrician and registered Republican.

Shull said he supported Hamilton because of his moderate political stances and because “he’s willing to talk to people.”

Speaking to Reuters after the event, Hamilton zeroed in on the message sent by voters like Shull in reliably ​Republican Kansas.

“It’s not just that Kansas is in play, and we might flip a seat,” Hamilton said. “It’s that people in a reliably red state are saying what’s happening in Washington, DC, is not OK.”

items.title: US to launch $8 billion support program for farmers to offset diesel costs, Trump says
items.content_html:
PARK CITY, Kansas, Oct 19 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Monday the US Department of Agriculture will launch what he called a new "harvest fuel relief program" that will provide farmers with $8 billion in support to ​offset diesel costs during the harvest season.

"Tonight, I'm also pleased to announce that the Department ​of Agriculture will be launching a new harvest fuel relief program, providing our ⁠farmers with $8 billion in support to offset diesel costs during this harvest season," Trump said ​in a midterm election campaign speech in Kansas.

The announcement was the latest in a series of financial promises and ​pledges that the Republican leader has made to voters heading into the November midterm elections, where control of Congress is at stake.

The Republican Party currently has a narrow majority in both the Senate and the House of Representatives. ​However, Trump's approval rating has been low due to his handling of the high cost of living ​for Americans during the US-Israeli war on Iran that has raised fuel prices.

Trump and the Republican Party have been scrambling ‌to ⁠maintain support in farm states with competitive Senate races as costs have risen.

Trump signed an executive order earlier this month that he said would expand access to tax-exempt diesel.

The Department of Agriculture said, opens new tab after Trump's speech on Monday that it would make $8 billion available "for one-time payments to American farmers this harvest ​season to provide relief during ​temporary market disruptions ⁠and increased input costs."

The program will provide what the department called "proportional support to producers using a uniform formula to cover a portion of modeled losses ​during the 2026 crop year."

The $8 billion in payments would be administered by ​the department's ⁠Farm Service Agency, the department said.

Trump has also separately proposed sending $5,000 checks to all adult citizens if Republicans keep control of the House and Senate in the midterms, though analysts, economists and even some ⁠Republicans in ​Congress have reacted with skepticism.

Earlier this month, Trump said the ​US government would send a one-time payment of $90 to more than 20 million Americans enrolled in Medicare, a health insurance program ​for the elderly.

items.title: Trump warns Kansans that US will 'burn' like France if Democrats win
items.content_html:
PARK CITY, Kansas, Oct 19 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump on Monday used violent unrest in France as an argument against Democrats in his battle ​to defend a Kansas Senate seat long held by Republicans but in danger of falling to his political opponents.

Trump's rally on behalf of Republican incumbent Roger Marshall was his latest ‌foray into conservative states where Republican candidates are on defense due to voter frustrations over the Iran war and rising prices.

"I love you Kansas, but I'm here for a guy named Roger Marshall," Trump said.

In a new addition to his stump speech, Trump pointed to widespread protests in France as a scenario that could erupt in the United States unless Republicans win. He provided no evidence.

France in recent days has seen some of the worst unrest in years as huge protests over the cost of living and ​underfunded public services descended into riots and looting.

Trump himself has struggled to make goods and services more affordable in the United States.

In his speech, Trump turned to anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim rhetoric, the type ​that he used to fuel his three presidential campaigns.

"We're not going to let that happen to this country," he said. "When you see burning steeples and raging fires in ⁠France, just remember that is what the radical Dumocrats want to do to America."

Trump has been mocking Democrats by calling them Dumocrats. Rights advocates have repeatedly criticized Trump for his rhetoric over the years in which he ​has targeted and mocked immigrants and ethnic minority groups. Civil rights groups say such rhetoric normalizes discriminatory attitudes towards those communities.

Kansas, a conservative Midwestern state Trump won by 16 points in 2024, has not elected a ​Democrat to the US Senate in 94 years. First-term Senator Marshall is in a close fight with Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton, pastor of a Methodist megachurch, who is running against Trump’s tariff agenda and what he calls the president's “erratic leadership.”

“He wants you to repent for being born White,” Trump said of Hamilton.

Marshall, in remarks to the rally, led his campaign argument on cultural issues like stopping "radical Islam." He called Hamilton "too woke" for Kansas because he supports gay pride parades, which the crowd loudly booed.

"We need ​someone who can sort heifers and steers," he said.

In response, Hamilton's campaign spokesperson called Marshall's campaign "sinking."

"Nothing said at the rally can distract from the fact Kansans are being crushed by rising gas and diesel prices, struggling to ​access affordable healthcare, and are tired of Washington corruption," the spokesperson, Tyson Brody, said.

In a Monday video, Hamilton welcomed Trump to the state and said his supporters have “a place” in his campaign. Hamilton said he will work with Trump when ‌it makes sense ⁠and stand up for Kansans when Washington policies hurt farmers and rural hospitals.

The tightness of the race is emblematic of the challenges looming for Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections as they try to defy political headwinds and retain control of the Senate and the House of Representatives.

Trump is deep into a 32-day campaign blitz, frequently going to friendly areas that he won handily in previous elections.

One Republican familiar with Trump's midterm strategy said the president’s attention on rural parts of the country is in response to internal polling showing soft support from men 55 years and younger in rural areas nationwide, a voting bloc crucial to Trump’s 2024 presidential win.

The latest ​Reuters/Ipsos poll, published on Monday, found that 31% of ​Americans approve of Trump's performance in office, a ⁠record low for the president.

Democrats need a net gain of four seats in both the US House of Representatives and US Senate to overturn Republicans' narrow 218-214 and 53-47 majorities.

In Park City, near Wichita, many rallygoers walked more than a mile across Interstate 135 to reach the rural arena, as a red-and-green truck stop sign flashed ​its latest prices above their heads: $3.98 for gas and $5.78 for diesel.

That is up about 45% compared to average gas prices in the state last year, according ​to motoring club AAA.

Economic concerns ⁠were palpable among Trump's most loyal supporters.

“Being on disability, I don’t have much, but it seems like the prices are still going up and they need to come down. It feels like you’re having to search or hunt for food," said Monique Mullen, 59, a Republican voter from Hutchinson, Kansas, who takes care of her father.

A small bloc of protesters gathered near the arena, including James Nightingale, a self-described independent from Halstead, Kansas.

“I’m a farmer from Kansas and the ⁠Trump administration has ​decimated the farm economy in my area. Not only have his tariffs decimated our markets for grain sales, now he is bringing ​in imported beef from outside the country. What happened to ‘America First’?” he said.

Kansans have proven a willingness to cross parties, as voters have elected a Democratic governor, Laura Kelly, for the last two terms. "I don't think it's ever easy to get elected here," said Gina ​Seman, a Trump voter from Towanda, Kansas, noting that Republican candidates in the past have taken their popularity for granted.

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: Trump's approval falls to record low of 31% as midterms near, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 19 (Reuters) - President Donald ‌Trump's approval rating fell to a record low as Americans worried about high gasoline prices and appeared ready to punish his Republican Party in the November 3 congressional elections, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll that closed on Monday.

Some 31% of Americans approve of Trump's ​performance in office, down a percentage point from two weeks earlier and the lowest level in ​either of his presidential terms, the four-day poll showed.

Asked which party they would vote ⁠for if the congressional elections were held today in what is known as a "generic ballot" question, some ​47% of registered voters in the nationwide poll picked Democrats and 35% chose Republicans. The 12-point Democratic advantage ​was the widest over the current election cycle and could bolster Democratic hopes of seizing control of the US House of Representatives and the US Senate.

For Republicans, losing control of either chamber could complicate Trump's agenda in the last two years ​of his term.

Generic ballot polls are national polls that provide an overall view of which party poll respondents ​want to see in charge in Congress. While these polls provide a view of national public sentiment, they do not ‌capture ⁠all the nuances of the state-by-state and district-by-district contests that determine control of the Senate and House, contests in which Republicans hold some structural advantages.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll two weeks earlier showed Democrats leading Republicans by 7 points, 44% to 37%.

Much of the drop in support for Republican congressional candidates was due to a larger ​share of women saying they ​would pick Democrats. Some ⁠50% of female voters said they would vote Democratic, compared to 32% eyeing Republican candidates. Men also favored Democrats, but by a smaller margin.

Trump's popularity has suffered ​since he ordered military strikes on Iran in February alongside US ally Israel. ​The war ⁠triggered a surge in gasoline prices, hitting household finances. Some 68% of Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of the economy, including 37% of self-identified Republicans.

Voters in the poll picked Democrats over Republicans as the better stewards of the ⁠economy, by ​40% to 33%.

The survey, which was conducted online, gathered responses ​from 1,679 US adults, including 1,279 registered voters. The poll's results had a margin of error of 2 percentage points for all respondents ​and 3 points for registered voters.

items.title: What you need to know about the 2026 US midterm elections
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, October 19 - Early voting has been underway for weeks ahead of the November 3, 2026, midterm elections, when US voters will elect members of the House of Representatives and Senate and governors in states across the country.

Held in the middle of each ​four-year presidential term, the midterms by definition do not involve the president. But for anyone who thinks they lack drama or importance this year, consider these two statistics:

More than 100 million people likely will ‌cast ballots in this year's midterm voting, if turnout is anything like the previous midterm in 2022; and as of October 12, a record $3.8 billion had been spent on political advertisements that have been aired so far. Top spending is in battleground US Senate races in Texas, Ohio and Michigan, according to AdImpact, which tracks the activities.

Elon Musk alone has spent about $366 million to support Republicans, according to campaign finance records.

Still, midterms generally attract fewer voters than the higher-profile presidential races. More than 155 million votes were cast in the 2024 presidential election, for example.

Plenty ​is at stake in this midterm election as Democrats try to win majority control of the US Congress.

Currently, Republicans hold a 218-214 majority in the House, where there are two vacancies and one independent who caucuses with Republicans. Democrats ​must win a net gain of four seats to win control.

Democrats also are fighting to win the Senate, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority. They must net four additional seats ⁠to get control. Ten races, including those in Maine, Ohio, North Carolina, Iowa and Georgia, could decide the outcome.

Midterm elections generally are dangerous territory for the political party that holds the White House and/or Congress. For 2026 that means ​that President Donald Trump and his Republicans controlling the US Senate and House of Representatives are in perilous political positions.

The midterms can be an opportunity for voters to, in effect, grade the president's performance, and possibly trigger White House course corrections if they receive ​low marks.

Midterm election results also can give aspiring presidential candidates hints on how to tailor their messages to voters in the next presidential campaign, which in this case will be in 2028.

Approval of Trump's performance is at an all-time low of 32%, according to a September Reuters/Ipsos poll.

Domestic issues like rising consumer prices are likely to have an impact on the outcome of many races and could erode support for Republicans.

At the same time, there is evidence that Democrats are more enthusiastic about voting this year than Republicans. If early voting trends continue it could point ​to a Democratic win in November.

There are also signs that Latino voters who veered to Trump in 2024 might be returning to Democrats because of frustration over the economy and some of Trump's immigration enforcement tactics.

However, a landslide for the Democrats is far from ​assured. Republicans could benefit from continued skepticism towards Democrats, a Republican spending advantage on campaigns, and fears from moderate voters over some primary wins by left-wingers.

Recent history tells the story of the shockwaves a midterm election can produce.

In the 2010 midterms, during the Democratic ‌presidency of Barack ⁠Obama, Republicans scored major victories, winning 63 additional House seats amid an underperforming US economy and weak support for Obama's landmark healthcare reform legislation. Democrats lost their majority. In the Senate, they held onto control despite losing six seats.

The Republican wave was a "shellacking," Obama lamented at the time. He subsequently faced Republican demands for significant reductions to non-defense spending.

Democrats returned the favor in 2018, with Trump in the White House. They gained a net total of 40 House seats, but lost a net two Senate seats.

This year's elections also have races for governors in 39 of the 50 states and voting in nearly every state for seats in their state-level legislative bodies.

Currently, Republicans control 55% of state legislative seats across the country, while Democrats hold 43.8%, according to Ballotpedia.

If Democrats manage to win the House, the next speaker — ​second in line for the presidency after the vice president — ⁠is likely to be Democratic Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York. He is currently the House Democratic leader.

Jeffries, who would become the first Black American to hold the powerful office, would be in a position to direct House committees to launch investigations into a range of controversial activities by Trump and his associates. Jeffries repeatedly has said Democrats would look into what he has ​called "unprecedented levels of corruption" during the Trump administration.

Jeffries also would steer Democrats' legislative priorities through the House. He has said Democrats would focus on making healthcare, groceries, housing, energy ​and other costs more affordable.

A Republican ⁠win, on the other hand, would ensure that the speaker's gavel remains in that party's hands, either with current speaker Mike Johnson or whichever Republican prevails if he is challenged for the job. Republican priorities are likely to be focused on additional tax cuts, huge increases in defense spending, and deeper social safety net reductions, building on Trump's 2025 "One Big Beautiful Bill."

Among the most-watched House races are Republican Representative Mike Lawler's bid for reelection to a New York district that Democratic candidate Kamala Harris won in her 2024 presidential ⁠campaign and an ​open seat in a Nebraska swing district where farmers and truckers face sharply higher fuel prices as a result of the US war against Iran.

Also ​high on Democrats' list of House seats they hope to take from Republicans are two in Pennsylvania and one in New Jersey.

Hovering over all of this are questions over whether Trump will try to meddle in the elections, which are administered by the 50 individual states.

Since 2020, he has repeatedly insisted there is ​widespread cheating in US elections, despite a lack of evidence. State election officials and Democrats in Congress have been preparing for possible legal challenges to any moves by his administration to try to intervene.

items.title: US Supreme Court to review 1868 federal ban on home distilling of liquor
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 19 (Reuters) - The Supreme Court agreed on Monday to decide the legality of a federal ​ban on the home distilling of alcoholic spirits that was enacted in 1868 after the US Civil War to ‌crack down on liquor tax evasion.

The dispute pits Republican President Donald Trump's administration, which is defending the law, against challengers who argue that the home-distilling prohibition exceeds the authority of Congress under the US Constitution. More than a dozen Republican-led states have backed the legal challenge to the statute.

The Supreme Court took up the ​administration's appeal of a lower court's decision against the ban. The justices are expected to hear arguments in the case and ​issue a ruling by the end of June.

Following the Civil War of 1861-1865, Congress sought to protect ⁠federal revenue by passing a law that banned home distilling. The current version of the law subjects violators to up to five years ​in prison and a $10,000 fine.

Challenges to the ban's legality have led to a split among lower federal courts of appeals.

In April, the New ​Orleans-based 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals declared the law unconstitutional, calling it an unnecessary and improper means for Congress to exercise its power to tax. Days later, the Cincinnati-based 6th US Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the constitutionality of the law, saying it was a "necessary and proper means" of collecting federal excise ​tax on distilled spirits.

The dueling decisions prompted appeals to the Supreme Court by the Justice Department and legal challengers.

Attorneys general from 15 Republican-led ​states, including Ohio, Florida and Idaho, filed a Supreme Court brief backing the challengers to the federal ban and urged the justices to resolve the ‌division, or "split," ⁠between the circuit courts of appeals.

"Unlike a good whiskey," the attorneys general wrote, "this split will not age well."

The 5th Circuit ruling was a legal victory for the nonprofit Hobby Distillers Association and 4 of its 1,300 members who argued in court papers that people should be free to distill spirits at home, whether as a hobby or for personal consumption.

Robert Alt, president and chief executive officer of the Buckeye Institute ​think tank and a lawyer for ​the challengers, expressed enthusiasm that ⁠his clients "will have their day in court."

"Our country's founders would be rolling over in their graves to learn that a pastime in which even George Washington partook, which is as American as apple pie and ​certainly a lot older, has quite absurdly been turned into a federal crime," Alt said.

The 5th ​Circuit upheld a ⁠2024 ruling by US District Judge Mark Pittman in Fort Worth, Texas. The ruling barred federal authorities from enforcing the ban against the plaintiffs in that case.

The Justice Department, urging the justices to take up the case, emphasized the importance of protecting federal revenue.

"Congress restricted home distilling 160 years ⁠ago in ​response to an extensive history of evasion of the distilled-spirits tax," Justice Department lawyers ​wrote.

"The government has a substantial interest in its authority to safeguard a significant source of tax revenue — a source that was used to pay Revolutionary War debts at ​the founding (of the nation) and now generates billions of dollars in tax revenue every year," they wrote.

items.title: USDA plans to resume imports of Mexican cattle at more ports of entry
items.content_html: CHICAGO, Oct 20 (Reuters) - The US Department of Agriculture plans to resume cattle ​imports from Mexico at two additional ‌US ports of entry, after halting shipments last year in an attempt to keep out ​the flesh-eating parasite New World ​screwworm, the agency said on Tuesday.

items.title: Rubio says Trump to take up to 60 days to weigh Russia sanctions
items.content_html:
Oct 17 (Reuters) - The day after waiving sanctions and tariffs related to ‌Russian exports, US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he has yet to announce a final decision on the matter, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said officials want more time to evaluate the situation.

Rubio said on Saturday that the president will use up to 60 days to assess the economic impact of Russia-related sanctions ​and tariffs that he waived a day earlier.

"A lot of you don't know what my decision is yet, but we'll figure ​it out, and you'll figure it out," Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida.

In ⁠a Truth Social post on Sunday, Trump wrote that his decision-making was aimed at avoiding anything "that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the ​bargaining table."

Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving key sanctions and tariffs under the law known as the Graham Act, which he signed ​last month at the urging of lawmakers who want to pressure Moscow over its war in Ukraine.

The measures, including tariffs on Russian goods and penalties on countries buying Russian oil and gas, were due to take effect next week. Friday's order did not specify how long the waiver would last, but Rubio said Trump opted ​for a 60-day review.

"I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions ​and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy," Rubio told reporters before boarding a plane for a trip to Uzbekistan.

Friday's executive ‌order drew ⁠criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, who warned it would embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin and prolong the war.

Rubio on Saturday also defended a separate US agreement with Russia to increase diesel supplies to global markets, aimed at easing fuel prices that have climbed amid the war with Iran and disruptions to energy supplies.

"That diesel is going to be sold one way or the other," Rubio said. "The only difference is how ​much of it the United States ​was going to get."

Under the agreement, ⁠Trump said Russia initially would supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the United States, followed by shipments in November and beyond.

The diesel agreement is "a carrot to try to end the war, not ​an economic lifeline" to Russia, US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said during a Sunday interview on ​ABC's "This Week."

But "the only way ⁠they can get additional diesel to export is if they turn down the conflict with Ukraine," Wright told CNN's "State of the Union" program on Sunday.

“If Russia can bring additional diesel to the market and export it, it would benefit American consumers,” he told CNN. “He's putting pressure that would both benefit ⁠American consumers ​and be a step forward for peace in the Russia-Ukraine war.”

Rubio said the diesel ​deal and sanctions waiver reflected the challenge of managing conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine that have disrupted global energy supplies.

"These conflicts around the world are starting to crash ​into each other," he said.

items.title: US Supreme Court will not review Trump's firing of labor board member
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 19 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court ​declined on Monday to hear a bid by a Democratic-appointed member of the National Labor ‌Relations Board to challenge the legality of her firing by President Donald Trump.

The justices turned away former NLRB member Gwynne Wilcox's appeal of a lower court's ruling that said the Republican president's January 2025 firing of her was a valid exercise ​of executive authority.

The court's action follows its June decision backing Trump's firing of Rebecca Slaughter, a ​Democratic Federal Trade Commission member.

That ruling overturned the court's 1935 precedent in a case ⁠called Humphrey's Executor that had recognized the authority of Congress to protect leaders of certain regulatory agencies ​from presidential removal at will. The Slaughter decision capped a decades-long conservative push to strengthen the president's ​grip on key levers of government power.

Trump's move to oust Wilcox from the NLRB was part of his shakeup and downsizing of the US government, including firing thousands of workers, dismantling federal agencies, installing loyalists in key jobs and purging ​career officials.

"I'm disappointed that the Supreme Court has declined to hear this case, not only for myself, ​but also for the workers and employers who rely on the National Labor Relations Board to resolve labor disputes impartially ‌and ⁠free from political pressure," Wilcox said in a statement.

Wilcox added that she would remain committed to "protecting the principles that allow the board to serve the public fairly."

The Justice Department declined to comment.

Wilcox, the first Black woman to serve on the agency's board, was appointed to a second five-year term in 2023 by Democratic ​former President Joe Biden. ​Trump moved to fire ⁠her about a week into his second presidential term, drawing a lawsuit by Wilcox. Slaughter also was a Biden appointee.

The legal fight over Trump's firing of Wilcox ​and other officials has figured as a key test of his efforts ​to bring federal ⁠agencies meant by Congress to be independent from the president under his control.

US District Judge Beryl Howell in March 2025 upheld a federal law protecting NLRB officials from being fired without cause, rejecting Trump's argument that ⁠the measure ​passed by Congress encroaches on authority granted to the president ​under the US Constitution.

That ruling was reversed in a 2-1 decision by the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia ​Circuit in December 2025, prompting Wilcox's appeal to the Supreme Court.

items.title: US CFTC secures order for ex-New York resident to pay $288 million
items.content_html: WASHINGTON, Oct 19 (Reuters) - The ​US Commodity ‌Futures Trading Commission ​said ​on Monday it ⁠secured court ​orders ​requiring a former New York ​resident ​and his firm ‌to ⁠pay more than $288 million ​for ​operating ⁠a commodity ​pool ​Ponzi ⁠scheme.

items.title: Senator Schumer urges FCC to reject conservative group's bid to use political AI-generated robocalls
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 19 (Reuters) - Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer on Monday urged the Federal Communications Commission not to approve a petition to allow political ​AI-generated robocalls from conservative political group Club for Growth ahead of the November ‌congressional elections.

"Under this change, campaigns could use their opponents’ voice to send out a message that is, at best, disingenuous and, at worst, a blatant lie," Schumer said.

The comment period expires on Monday.

FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, ​a Democrat who has opposed the petition, said Monday on CNN the FCC could ​act in the coming days and just two weeks ahead of the ⁠Nov. 3 election.

A spokesperson for the FCC said the agency is not planning to ​grant the petition. "There is no one at the FCC that has expressed any interest in moving ​to an order on this or any of the petitions and there are zero plans to so," the spokesperson said.

"There is absolutely no excuse to relax these standards and allow special interests to flood our cellphone ​lines with deepfakes or dark-money-funded AI voices," Schumer said.

The group, which is spending millions of ​dollars ahead of the November US congressional elections, earlier asked the FCC to allow it to make political calls to cell ‌phones "using ⁠an artificial or prerecorded voice - including an AI-generated voice - without obtaining prior express consent."

Club for Growth President David McIntosh said in a statement earlier this month that the group wants "the FCC to treat First Amendment-protected political speech the same way it already treats wireless calls about package deliveries, bank accounts, ​and doctor's appointments."

The group, ​which backs conservative ⁠economic views on taxes, regulations and cutting the size of government, plans to spend $175 million in the midterm congressional elections, it said on its ​website.

The FCC, in describing the petition, said the system "uses a perfunctory ​human being for ⁠the sole purpose of clicking on a ‘send’ or similarly termed button to transmit thousands of text messages per hour."

A number of public interest groups have urged the FCC not to grant ⁠the petition.

​Schumer noted that in 2024, the FCC proposed fining ​a political consultant $6 million over fake robocalls that mimicked then President Joe Biden's voice, urging New Hampshire voters not to ​vote in that state's Democratic primary.

items.title: US Supreme Court to hear Maryland case involving race in school admissions
items.content_html:
Oct 19 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court agreed on Monday to consider reviving a lawsuit against a Maryland county's lottery admissions policy for four ​elite public middle schools that some parents claim unlawfully discriminates against Asian American applicants.

Delving again into the contentious issue of race in student admissions, the ‌justices took up an appeal by a coalition of parents of a lower court's decision rejecting their claim that Montgomery County's policy violates the US Constitution's 14th Amendment guarantee of equal protection under the law.

The Supreme Court is expected to hear the case and rule by the end of June.

The parents sued to challenge the entrance policies for the county's academically rigorous "magnet" schools, which provide enrichment programs in math and science, ​or the humanities, for high-achieving students in sixth through eighth grades. They include Takoma Park Middle School in Silver Spring and Martin Luther King Jr. Middle School in ​Germantown.

The case represents the latest legal attack on entrance policies at certain highly selective public schools that challengers critique for continuing to pursue "racial ⁠balancing" with the aim of boosting diversity.

The Supreme Court issued a landmark 2023 ruling that rejected race-conscious college and university admissions policies long used to raise the number of Black, Hispanic and ​other minority students on campuses.

Plaintiffs in these new legal challenges claim that admissions to these prestigious programs, though race-neutral on the surface, use proxies such as socioeconomic status to achieve the ​same unlawful, race-based result in pursuit of diversity.

The legal challenges coincide with President Donald Trump's policies, implemented since he returned to office last year, against diversity, equity and inclusion, or DEI, programs in education, as well as in the US government and military, and in private companies.

At issue in the Maryland case is whether lower courts may dismiss claims of intentional racial discrimination if the policy has not disproportionately harmed that racial ​group, in this instance Asian American students.

Montgomery County is a wealthy suburb of Washington, DC.

The parent coalition, called the Association for Education Fairness, is represented by the Pacific Legal Foundation, ​a libertarian legal group that has pursued similar challenges in Virginia and Massachusetts. The Supreme Court rejected those cases in 2024.

"The Constitution protects students as individuals, not as members of a racial group," said Chris Kieser, ‌an attorney ⁠for the coalition.

"A school district should not be able to defeat a discrimination claim by showing that its policy did not harm enough Asian American children. Every family deserves admissions rules that judge their child on their own merit," Kieser said.

A spokesperson for Montgomery County Public Schools said the school district "remains committed to providing equitable access to rigorous opportunities for all students. This commitment will continue uninterrupted as the judicial process proceeds."

The Montgomery County school district's selection process was introduced in the 2021-2022 school year, during the COVID-19 pandemic. It screens all students ​for academic potential, and then implements a ​lottery to randomly assign students from that ⁠pool to receive enriched instruction at either a magnet school or a local school.

The lawsuit said that the lottery system led to a lower number of Asian American student placements at the magnet schools.

The suit alleged that the screening process makes it harder for Asian American ​students, who the challengers said are clustered in "high-performing, low-poverty elementary schools," to enter the lottery pool. Part of the process ranks a ​student's performance by comparing the ⁠student's test scores against those of other students whose family incomes are at a similar level.

US District Judge Paula Xinis threw out the case in 2022, finding that the policy did not place a disproportionate burden on Asian American students. The judge noted that the percentage of admitted Asian American students exceeded the percentage of Asian Americans among all applicants to the magnet schools. Xinis ⁠also found ​that there was no evidence that the lottery policy was implemented with discriminatory intent.

The Richmond, Virginia-based 4th US Circuit ​Court of Appeals upheld the dismissal, agreeing that the lawsuit "does not plausibly allege that the challenged policy disparately impacts Asian American students."

The Supreme Court's 2023 affirmative action ruling upended decades of precedent, striking down programs used by Harvard ​University and the University of North Carolina that took race into account as one of many factors in student admissions evaluations.

items.title: US Supreme Court snubs bid to revive plea deal for accused 9/11 mastermind
items.content_html:
Oct 19 (Reuters) - The US ​Supreme Court declined on Monday to hear a bid by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind ‌of the September 11, 2001, attacks, to revive a 2024 agreement that would have spared him the death penalty in exchange for a guilty plea — a deal scrapped by former Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin.

The justices turned away appeals by Mohammed and two co-defendants who had ​also signed plea agreements of a lower court's ruling that upheld Austin's decision to void the deals. ​The US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit rejected an argument that ⁠Austin, who served under former President Joe Biden, had acted too late.

The Supreme Court's action marks the latest ​milestone in a military prosecution of the detainees held in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, that has been beset by two decades ​of legal gridlock.

In August, a US Air Force judge set the trial for Mohammed and his co-defendants for June 2028.

Mohammed remains the most well-known inmate at the Guantanamo detention facility, which was set up in 2002 by then-US President George W. Bush to house ​foreign terrorism suspects following the 9/11 attacks, which killed nearly 3,000 people. Mohammed is accused of orchestrating the plot ​to fly hijacked passenger jetliners into the World Trade Center in New York City and into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia.

Monday's Supreme ⁠Court action "clears the path for holding those responsible for the September 11 attacks accountable. This is a critical step toward delivering justice for the victims and families on one of the darkest days in American history," a US Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement.

The plea agreements for Mohammed and co-defendants Mustafa al Hawsawi and Walid bin 'Atash had ​been offered and accepted by ​the US official overseeing ⁠the Pentagon's Guantanamo war court, prompting criticism by Republican lawmakers.

Austin revoked the deals two days later.

A military judge ruled that Austin lacked authority to invalidate the plea deals in a ​decision that was upheld in December by the US Court of Military Commission Review. The ​judge then scheduled ⁠prompt plea hearings.

The DC Circuit paused those proceedings, and in July 2025, a panel of that court — in a 2-1 vote — backed the decision to scrap the plea deals, saying that Austin "indisputably had legal authority to withdraw from the agreements."

Defense ⁠attorneys for ​Mohammed and al Hawsawi, including lawyers from the American Civil Liberties ​Union, had urged the Supreme Court to hear the case. They said Austin's action violated controlling military law and "prolonged the best chance for finality ​in the September 11 case in a quarter century."

items.title: US military weighs use of ‘mother of all bombs’ in potential future strikes on Iran, CNN says
items.content_html:
Oct 15 (Reuters) - The US military has developed strike plans ​that could include using ‌the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, also known ​as the "mother of ​all bombs", against Iranian energy ⁠infrastructure and nuclear sites ​if President Donald Trump ​orders renewed combat operations, CNN reported on Thursday citing US ​officials familiar with the ​matter.

The potential deployment of the largest ‌non-nuclear ⁠bomb in the US arsenal would mark a significant escalation in the ​conflict, ​although ⁠officials familiar with military planning discussions ​told CNN questions remain ​over ⁠its effectiveness in achieving Washington's strategic objectives.

Reuters could ⁠not ​immediately verify the ​report.

items.title: Driver released after pickup truck kills 2, injures 10 at Kansas youth soccer game
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Oct 18 (Reuters) - The woman who was driving a pickup truck that entered a Kansas soccer field during ​a youth match, killing a man and 6-year-old boy, was ‌released without charges while the investigation continues, authorities said on Sunday.

Investigators interviewed the 34-year-old woman, whom authorities have not publicly identified, and consulted ​with the Sedgwick County district attorney's office before releasing ​her, the Wichita Police Department said in a statement.

Police ⁠said toxicology testing and a mechanical examination of the vehicle ​were still under way.

The Chevrolet pickup truck had been parked near ​a soccer field in Wichita on Saturday before entering the pitch during a game and striking multiple people, police said.

Five children ages 5 to ​9 and five adults suffered noncritical injuries, police said.

Two children ​of the driver were inside the truck when the incident occurred and ‌were ⁠interviewed, police said. One of the driver's children was playing on a different soccer field at the complex, according to the police statement.

Wichita police will present an initial review of the ​case to the ​district attorney early ⁠this week, district attorney's office spokesperson Lyndsee Stover said in an email.

Police identified those killed ​in the crash as 6-year-old Cole Adrian and ​35-year-old Nicholas ⁠Schafer of McPherson, Kansas.

"Our hearts are with the families of Adrian and Nicholas as they face an unimaginable loss. What should ⁠have been ​a day of children playing soccer ​and families spending time together ended in tragedy," Wichita Police Chief Joe Sullivan ​said.

items.title: Anthropic to add US voting information to Claude before midterms
items.content_html:
Oct 14 (Reuters) - (This Oct 14 story has been corrected to say that chats about whom or what to vote for accounted for 0.01% of US conversations, not requests for recommendations on how to vote, in paragraph 7.)

Anthropic said on Wednesday it would add official US voting information from nonprofit Democracy Works and ​election results to its Claude AI chatbot ​later this month, ahead of the November midterms.

The ⁠AI company said its goal was to position ​Claude as a useful tool for political conversations, while ​preventing election-related abuse.

"Today, conversations that touch broadly on politics, public policy or social issues account for about 5.75% of all ​conversations in the United States on Claude.ai, our ​consumer app," the company said in a statement, citing analysis of ‌250,000 ⁠US conversations.

The move comes as AI companies increasingly position chatbots as sources of news and information, potentially helping Anthropic draw more users during the election cycle.

About ​0.51% of ​Claude conversations ⁠are specifically about elections or voting, Anthropic said, adding that it expects political ​and election-related queries to rise as election ​day ⁠approaches.

Later this month, US users seeking voting logistics will receive answers drawn directly from Democracy Works' database of ⁠state ​and local election sources.

Anthropic said chats on ​whom or what to vote for were 0.01% of U.S. conversations.

items.title: Top cases on the US Supreme Court's docket
items.content_html:
October 19 - The US Supreme Court is hearing a series of important cases during its current nine-month term involving issues such as President Donald Trump's immigration policies, asylum, assault-style rifle bans, race, Big Oil's role in climate change, Republican-backed voting restrictions, LGBT rights and more.

Here is a look at some of the cases being argued during the term, which runs to about the end of June.

The justices wrestled with complex questions over whether to let local governments try to hold oil companies liable for the harms caused by climate change during October 5 ​arguments in a bid by ExxonMobil (XOM.N), opens new tab and Suncor Energy (SU.TO), opens new tab to thwart a lawsuit by officials in Boulder, Colorado. The companies appealed after Colorado's top court allowed Boulder's lawsuit accusing them of violating state law and seeking unspecified monetary damages. The Trump administration backed the ‌companies. The justices voiced concerns about unduly limiting the authority of states to pursue climate-related litigation, as well as the potential to unleash chaos if local governments across the country were permitted to sue these companies. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

The court will decide the legality of Trump's policy that subjects millions of immigrants in the US illegally to mandatory detention during deportation proceedings. The policy is part of Trump's pursuit of mass deportation. The justices took up the Trump administration's appeal of a lower court's ruling against the policy in a case involving a Brazilian national. The administration abandoned the US government's longstanding interpretation of federal law that immigrants already living in the US could be released on bond while their ​cases play out in immigration court. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

The justices will hear arguments in December over the Trump administration's policy of deporting migrants to nations other than their own — so-called "third countries" — without ​offering them the chance to show the harms they may face. The court on September 29 let the administration continue the policy for the time being, putting on hold a federal judge's ruling that removing migrants to third countries ⁠is unlawful. More than 25,000 migrants have been deported to 29 countries under the policy, according to human rights groups. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

The court will hear the Trump administration's bid to deny asylum to a man who was forced to prepare meals for an apparent separatist ​group in Nigeria — a case that could expand what officials may deem terrorist activity under American immigration law. The Justice Department appealed a lower court's ruling in favor of Nigerian citizen Izuchukwu Ozurumba. He was denied US asylum due to his work cooking for a group known as the Unknown Gunmen that US officials considered to be ​a terrorist organization. The lower court ruled that cooking did not qualify as "material support" for terrorism under the immigration statute. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

The justices will hear arguments on December 2 in a challenge to the legality of state prohibitions on assault-style rifles, giving them another chance to expand gun rights in a case that involves a type of weapon often associated with mass shootings.
