Lower courts upheld bans in Cook County, Illinois, and Connecticut on powerful semiautomatic rifles such as AR-15s. The lower courts rejected arguments that the measures violate the US Constitution's Second Amendment right to "keep and bear arms." Gun rights groups and other challengers have ​said that Supreme Court precedents concerning the Second Amendment protect these firearms, which they described as in "common use." A ruling is expected by the end of June.

The justices will hear arguments on December 8 in a Republican-led bid to revive voter restrictions in Arizona that would stiffen proof-of-citizenship requirements for voter registrants and purge ​state voter rolls of alleged non-US citizens. Republicans appealed after a lower court halted provisions of Arizona's law because they were found to violate a federal voting registration statute. President Donald Trump's administration has backed key elements of the appeal. Critics have said the Arizona measure adds extra mandates for voting that unfairly target Latino, Native American and student voters. ‌Those groups tend to ⁠favor Democratic candidates. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

The justices will consider whether to revive a lawsuit against a Maryland county's lottery admissions policy for four elite public middle schools that some parents claim unlawfully discriminates against Asian American applicants. The case has the court delving again into the contentious issue of race in student admissions. A coalition of parents appealed a lower court's decision rejecting their claim that Montgomery County's policy violates the US Constitution's 14th Amendment guarantee of equal protection under the law. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

The justices will hear arguments on November 3 in a bid by the Archdiocese of Denver and other Catholic entities to be exempted from a Colorado preschool funding program's nondiscrimination requirement. A lower court found that Colorado's program did not violate the religious rights of the Catholic plaintiffs under the US Constitution's First Amendment. The program provides state funds ​for preschools. The Catholic plaintiffs objected to the state's requirement that schools receiving ​funding under the program give all children "equal opportunity" to enroll in preschool ⁠regardless of certain characteristics, including the sexual orientation or gender identity of students or their family members. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

The justices will decide whether the Trump administration can avoid handing over records to a watchdog group about its Department of Government Efficiency, an initiative aimed at slashing agency budgets and workers spearheaded last year by the president's former adviser Elon Musk. The administration appealed a judge's order for DOGE to respond to requests by Citizens for ​Responsibility and Ethics in Washington for information about its operations. The judge found that DOGE likely is a government agency covered by the federal Freedom of Information Act, or FOIA. The date for the arguments has not yet ​been announced. A ruling is expected by the ⁠end of June.

The court will decide the legality of a federal ban on the home distilling of alcoholic spirits that was enacted in 1868 after the US Civil War to crack down on liquor tax evasion. The dispute pits the Trump administration, which is defending the law, against challengers who argue that the home-distilling prohibition exceeds the authority of Congress under the US Constitution. More than a dozen Republican-led states have backed the legal challenge to the statute. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

The justices will hear Apple's (AAPL.O), opens new tab bid to escape being found in contempt in its legal ⁠fight with "Fortnite" maker Epic ​Games after the iPhone maker was deemed in violation of a judicial order mandating sweeping changes to its lucrative App Store in the antitrust litigation. Apple appealed a lower court's ruling upholding a ​decision by an Oakland, California-based federal judge finding Apple in contempt in Epic's 2020 lawsuit contesting App Store fees. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

The court will hear arguments in a bid by canned-coffee maker Rise Brewing to hold PepsiCo (PEP.O), opens new tab liable for alleged trademark infringement concerning Pepsi's morning energy drink "Mtn Dew Rise." Rise ​appealed a lower court's ruling rejecting the company's claim that the product name "Mtn Dew Rise" infringes its trademarks and creates customer confusion with its coffee brand. The date for the arguments has not yet been announced. A ruling is expected by the end of June.

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: US Justice Department threatens California over alleged noncitizen voters, letters show
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department on Tuesday gave California officials 48 hours to review a list of alleged noncitizen voters or face ‌legal action, according to two letters reviewed by Reuters, part of an unprecedented effort to find evidence of voter fraud ahead of next month's elections.

The letters, written by acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter and addressed to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan, say the Justice Department provided officials in Los Angeles County with a "password-protected thumb drive" with the names of people ​the federal government "believes are likely noncitizens" and were sent mail-in ballots from California.

The letters demand that the state and county segregate returned mail-in ballots from voters ​on the Justice Department's list and not tabulate their votes "until citizenship has been determined." In cases where ballots have not been sent out ⁠yet, it orders California officials to withhold them from those on the list until their citizenship is confirmed.

The federal government "will have no choice but to seek emergency relief," according ​to the letters, if state and county officials do not follow its instructions.

"Allowing noncitizens to vote cancels citizen votes," McCotter wrote.

The letters mark an escalation of the Trump administration's attempts to ​pressure states over alleged voting by non-US citizens and signal the Justice Department may be prepared to challenge ballots in the weeks leading up to the November 3 election, when Republicans will be defending their narrow majorities in Congress.

Justice Department spokeswoman Kiersten Pels confirmed the existence of the letters in a statement to Reuters, adding: "The department will take all necessary legal action to protect election integrity and ensure ​compliance with federal law.”

Representatives from the White House and the California secretary of state's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Logan also did not immediately respond.

The Justice Department under President Donald Trump has repeatedly claimed that voting by non-US citizens is widespread, despite multiple studies showing it is rare.

Though states may have added more than 30,000 noncitizens to their voter ‌rolls since ⁠2000 due to software glitches and clerical errors, Reuters found in September, it was unclear how many had cast a ballot. Experts said the numbers were too small relative to the country’s 170 million registered voters to affect elections.

In July, the Justice Department sent letters to chief election officials in all 50 states warning they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls or cast ballots.

The department's Civil Rights Division has demanded nonpublic voter data, including voters' Social Security numbers or dates of birth, ​from nearly all states as part of its ​hunt for noncitizens on state rolls. ⁠It has sued 30 Democratic- and Republican-led states that refused to hand over their rolls, but has lost 26 of those cases without winning one.

Reuters reported last month that the Department of Homeland Security was using a commercial data broker to find sensitive voter information not included in ​publicly available rolls, which officials and experts warned could lead to citizens being falsely flagged as illegal voters and potentially detained.

Federal ​prosecutors have also ramped up ⁠prosecutions of noncitizens for allegedly voting in past elections or submitting fraudulent registrations, touting 16 new criminal cases on Monday.

Officials in Democratic-led California have tussled for months with the Trump administration over its attempts to intervene in election procedures over allegations of voter fraud.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin informed California officials on July 16 that the federal government believed the state had noncitizens ⁠on its voting ​rolls, according to the letter.

California could prove pivotal in deciding control of the US House of Representatives, ​especially after the state's voters approved a new congressional map that heavily favors Democrats as part of a nationwide redistricting sprint that began in Republican-led states.

Voters in Los Angeles will also weigh in on a ballot measure ​that would allow certain noncitizen legal residents to cast ballots in municipal elections.

items.title: Trump faults aides as Republican midterm prospects dim
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 17 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump is blaming senior aides and political operatives for a faltering midterm strategy, questioning campaign spending, faulting redistricting and second-guessing candidate choices as Republicans fight to retain control of Congress, said three people familiar with internal discussions.

Trump is not on the November 3 ballot but repeatedly tells supporters ​to pretend that he is, hoping to mobilize voters who might otherwise skip the election. He has embarked on a frenetic campaign schedule while largely avoiding acknowledging his own role in shaping ‌the strategy and how his unpopularity is weighing on Republican candidates in competitive races.

Much of the friction has centered on James Blair, the longtime aide who runs Trump's super PAC MAGA Inc., and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who until now had largely escaped criticism. Trump has faulted Blair's handling of campaign funds, while some White House officials and allies have questioned Wiles' oversight of the political operation.

As Trump questions why campaign spending has failed to improve Republican polling numbers, his advisers are also blaming one another. Wiles has pointed to Blair, ​while Blair has faulted the White House legislative affairs team, one of the people said.

"What's really happening is a circular firing squad," the person said.

Opinion polls suggest Democrats will win the House of Representatives, while the ​Senate remains too close to call. Losing the House would hamper Trump's legislative agenda in the final two years of his term and give Democrats subpoena power to investigate ⁠his administration.

Trump defended Wiles on Friday, calling her "smart" and "tough" and saying she would remain in her job. "Susie is here, and she's going to be here for a long time," he said.

White House spokesman Davis Ingle rejected the sources' characterization, ​saying they were "armchair experts peddling their baseless speculation." Wiles did not respond to a request for comment.

Trump has long sought to distance himself from political setbacks. He refused to accept his defeat in the ​2020 election and said ahead of the 2022 midterm results that he deserved "all the credit" if Republicans won but "should not be blamed at all" if they lost. More recently, he has reminded audiences that the president's party typically struggles in midterm elections.

But Trump helped devise and drive some of the strategies he is now questioning, including the redistricting effort and candidate choices shaped by his personal loyalties or grievances. His approval rating is at the lowest point of his presidency, weighed down by voter concern over high prices and dissatisfaction with the ​Iran war.

Trump's frustrations with his political team spilled into public view after Blair and Chris LaCivita, who co-managed Trump's 2024 campaign, traveled in early October to Republika Srpska, a self-governing region of Bosnia. The New York Times reported the ​men received substantial payments to advise the regional government ahead of local elections.

Trump distanced himself from both men, describing them as "outside consultants" in an October 7 Truth Social post and warning that if he found a conflict of interest, he would "terminate them, immediately!"

Senior White ‌House officials questioned ⁠why Blair was taking on lucrative work overseas when he was supposed to be overseeing the final stretch of the Republican campaign, three people said.

One person said Wiles approved the trip without informing Trump, raising questions about how closely she was overseeing his political advisers.

For Trump, the larger concern is that Blair's outside work has distracted him from his political responsibilities, two people said.

In a statement, Blair said: "All of this mudslinging is ridiculous, and counterproductive. President Trump and me are focused on helping Republicans win in November. Every other Republican should be doing the same."

In a separate statement, LaCivita said: "President Trump and his team are and always have been focused on the midterms. That's demonstrated through the money, message and motivation that ​the president is bringing on the road and all year. ​Sniping from unnamed cowards who've never been in a ⁠fight is not worth responding to."

With Trump asking why Republican polling in pivotal races has not improved despite MAGA Inc.'s campaign spending, which public records put at $200 million so far, it remains unclear whether he will approve more spending before the election, one of the sources said.

Trump also has pressed political aides and advisers in the past ​week to explain why the redistricting effort he personally pushed has failed to deliver more clear-cut Republican gains, two sources said.

Texas is a particular concern. Republicans redrew the ​state's congressional map to gain seats, ⁠but the strategy relies in part on Hispanic voters turning out as they did for the 2024 election. Opinion polls suggest that support may be difficult to replicate amid concerns about the cost of living and Trump's handling of the economy. Some Republicans fear the new boundaries could backfire, leaving incumbents more vulnerable instead of giving the party an advantage.

"The redistricting diced up the Trump voters too much," one of the sources said.

Trump had said Blair was expected to return to the White House after ⁠the midterms, describing ​his departure as a "short leave of absence." But two sources said his return was now unlikely. "He's not coming back. That is not happening," one ​of them said.

It was less clear how things would play out for Wiles, who played a central role in Trump's 2024 victory and has been credited by Trump allies and aides with bringing greater discipline to his White House in his second term.

Trump "may be annoyed at certain things but ​she has effectively kept that machine going," a fourth source close to the White House said.

items.title: Trump threatens California officials with imprisonment over stance on mail ballots
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 16 (Reuters) - (This Oct 16 story has been repeated with no changes to the text.)

The US Justice Department on Friday warned ​Los Angeles County and California election officials they could be liable as abettors of a federal ‌crime if they count mail ballots returned by more than 20,000 people the Trump administration says are probably noncitizens.

The warning to the Los Angeles County Assistant Counsel Peter Bollinger came less than three weeks before the November 3 midterm elections and days after the department gave California 48 ​hours to review a list of alleged noncitizen voters or face legal action. On Thursday, the Justice Department sued ​California to block the state from counting the ballots.

"Noncitizen voting in a federal election is ⁠a federal crime — and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful," Trent McCotter, the acting US deputy attorney general, ​wrote in a letter released on Friday. McCotter called on the county and California's secretary of state to reconsider their refusal ​to take steps that the Trump administration argues are needed to deter voter fraud.

US President Donald Trump shared the letter on Truth Social with the comment: "They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!"

California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County ​Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan were copied on McCotter's letter.

The county's counsel office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Weber's ​office referred Reuters to an earlier statement in which she said the Justice Department's attempts to "unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter ‌data and ⁠purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections."

An earlier letter that McCotter sent on Tuesday to Weber and Logan said the Justice Department provided officials in Los Angeles County with a "password-protected thumb drive" with the names of people the federal government "believes are likely noncitizens" that were sent mail-in ballots from California.

Los Angeles County Counsel ​Dawyn R. Harrison said on ​Thursday the county cannot ⁠comply with the Justice Department's requests because the Trump administration did not explain how the list was made. Friday's letter from McCotter said the Justice Department used "internal immigration records" and ​data matching.

In July, Trump said his administration had uncovered evidence of more than 275,000 non-citizens registered ​to vote, ⁠but it was not clear how many had actually voted.

In some previous cases, systems intended to verify citizenship have mistakenly flagged some naturalized US citizens as noncitizens. Studies have found that noncitizens casting actual ballots is exceedingly uncommon.

Since July, the Justice Department ⁠has ramped up ​prosecutions of people accused of illegally voting while not holding US citizenship. ​The White House has also pushed federal agencies to accelerate their review of at least 47 state voter rolls obtained by the Department of Homeland Security, ​according to an internal email seen by Reuters.

items.title: Trump mocks popularity of the name Mohammad, common among Muslims
items.content_html:
DALTON, Georgia, Oct 16 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump made a joke about the popularity of the name Mohammad in the Muslim world ​as he mocked Iran's presidency during a campaign speech on Friday.

"You ‌know, if you're in doubt about somebody's name from the Middle East, just say 'Mohammad,'" Trump told a crowd in Dalton, Georgia. "You have about a 65% chance. 'Hello, Mohammad.' I've done it ​for years now. I've never been wrong."

Mohammad is one of the most ​common male names among Muslims, who often name their sons after ⁠the Prophet Mohammad, the founder of Islam.

Trump made the comment as he ​was discussing Iran during a rally in a hangar at Dalton Municipal Airport ​in Georgia, where he campaigned for Republican political candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

"Iran is the only country where nobody wants to be president," Trump said, then pretended to ​ask several people named Mohammad whether they wanted the job. Masoud Pezeshkian ​has been president of Iran since 2024.

The Georgia crowd gave the joke a muted response.

Rights advocates ‌and ⁠Muslim advocacy groups have repeatedly criticized Trump for rhetoric that they say demonizes and mocks Muslims, immigrants and ethnic minorities.

He has escalated such rhetoric during the midterm campaign season, particularly against Somali and Muslim Americans including Muslim Democratic US Senate ​candidate Abdul El-Sayed ​and Representative Ilhan ⁠Omar, a Minnesota Democrat who came to the US as a Somali refugee.

Trump repeated his vow that Iran would never ​get a nuclear weapon, seven months after the United States ​and Israel ⁠launched a war on Tehran aimed in part at crippling its nuclear program.

An annual report by the Council on American Islamic Relations released earlier this year attributed rising ⁠Islamophobia ​in the US in part to Trump's crackdown ​on immigration and pro-Palestinian protests during his second term.
